strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and timely problem: existing fidelity/coverage metrics (Density, Coverage, and many recent variants) lack robustness to outliers and interpretable absolute scores, an issue explicitly highlighted by a recent position paper (Räisä et al., 2025). The paper directly tackles this open challenge.

The proposed fixes are simple, principled, and well-motivated: capping individual sample contributions to 1 and clipping ball radii to the median NND for Clipped Density; using constant-mass balls with capped per-sample contribution for Clipped Coverage. The intuition is clearly illustrated with a toy example (Figure 2).

Rigorous theoretical treatment: Lemma 1 derives a closed-form expected value of ClippedCoverage_unnorm under the null (identical distributions) using a Beta-Binomial argument, which is then used to calibrate the metric for linear degradation. The proof is detailed and appears correct.

Extensive empirical validation across many controlled scenarios (mode dropping, OOD sample injection, distribution translation, mixture tests) on both synthetic and real (CIFAR-10) data, with comparisons against a large number of baselines (Precision/Recall, Density/Coverage, symPrecision/symRecall, α-Precision/β-Recall, TopP&R, P-precision/P-recall, Precision/Recall Cover). Clipped Density/Coverage are the only metrics passing all tests.

Strong reproducibility efforts: reimplementation details, complexity analysis showing improved memory scaling (O(Nd) vs O(N^2)), verification that reimplementations match original code outputs exactly, and detailed compute/resource reporting.

Thorough appendix material: real-world case studies (e.g., RESFLOW CIFAR-10 outliers inflating Density, chest X-ray GAN evaluation demonstrating absolute interpretability), a component-wise ablation (Table 3–6) isolating the effect of each modification, sensitivity analysis to hyperparameter k, and an honest, detailed comparison against the Räisä et al. sanity-check benchmark, including candid discussion of cases where the paper's own metrics fail or where they contest the benchmark's criteria.

Practical significance demonstrated via evaluation of many real generative models (CIFAR-10, ImageNet, LSUN, FFHQ) showing consistent, interpretable trends (diffusion > GAN, dataset-size correlation with achievable scores), illustrating real utility for practitioners assessing absolute model quality.
weaknesses: The interpretability claim ("score x means equivalent to x proportion of good samples") is calibrated specifically against a scenario of purely random/OOD 'bad' samples; it's unclear how this interpretation generalizes to more realistic failure modes (e.g., subtle mode collapse, minor distributional shift, blurry-but-plausible samples) rather than obviously out-of-distribution noise.

Clipped Coverage's calibration procedure (numerical inversion of fexpected via sorting, Section 4.2.2) is somewhat ad hoc/non-closed-form compared to Clipped Density's simpler real-data normalization; the general applicability and stability of this calibration across very different dataset sizes/dimensionalities is not deeply analyzed.

The paper's own benchmark comparison against Räisä et al. (2025) in Appendix H reveals a non-trivial number of failures for Clipped Density/Coverage (e.g., 'Discrete Num. vs Continuous Num.', 'Hypercube Varying Sample/Syn Size', several Bounds tests), and the paper argues some of the benchmark's failure criteria are 'too harsh' or 'incorrect' — this self-serving reinterpretation of failing cases could be seen as weakening the objectivity of the evaluation.

The choice of k (number of nearest neighbors) remains a manual hyperparameter; although Appendix K shows relative stability, no principled method for selecting k is proposed, and all main experiments use a single fixed k=5.

Reliance on a single embedding space (DINOv2-L) for all real-image experiments; the paper acknowledges but does not empirically explore sensitivity of Clipped Density/Coverage to the choice of embedding model, which is known to meaningfully affect metric rankings (per Stein et al. 2023).

No user study or downstream task validation connecting the proposed 'interpretable' scores to actual perceptual quality or practical utility judgments — the interpretability claim rests on synthetic calibration/definition rather than external validation.

Some presentation clutter: heavy reliance on an extensive appendix (37 pages) for core supporting evidence (e.g., proofs, ablations, benchmark comparisons) makes the main text feel like a summary of a much larger body of work, and readers must consult appendices extensively to fully evaluate claims.

strengths: Addresses a well-recognized and important problem: the lack of robust, interpretable fidelity/coverage metrics for generative models, directly responding to the recent position paper (Räisä et al., 2025) that argues all current metrics are flawed.

Clean, well-motivated methodological contribution: clipping individual sample contributions to bound outlier influence, plus clipping nearest-neighbor ball radii (for fidelity) to avoid large-volume outlier balls dominating the score.

Rigorous theoretical support: Lemma 1 derives the exact expected value of unnormalized Clipped Coverage under the i.i.d. null via a Beta-Binomial argument, enabling a principled empirical calibration that yields the desired linear degradation property, which is proven and clearly presented (Appendix A/B).

Extensive and carefully designed empirical validation: dozens of controlled synthetic/toy tests (mode dropping, mode collapse, outlier injection, distribution translation, rare modes, incorrect correlations), evaluation on four real image datasets with ~46 generative models, a medical imaging (chest X-ray) case study demonstrating absolute (reference-free) interpretability, human-judgment correlation analysis, sensitivity to hyperparameter k, sample-size stability analysis, and even non-image modalities (music, time series).

Strong reproducibility and transparency: detailed implementation/complexity comparisons against prior metric implementations (with exact score reproduction and efficiency gains), computational cost reporting, and code release.

Honest engagement with limitations and counter-evidence, including candidly reporting a non-significant correlation with human judgment on FFHQ and providing a detailed, self-critical comparison against the Räisä et al. benchmark rather than only favorable cherry-picked results.
The interpretability framing (score = proportion of good vs. bad samples) is intuitive and operationalized in a testable, quantitative way rather than left as a vague claim.
weaknesses: The core technical idea (clipping per-sample contributions to at most 1, and clipping ball radii to a median value) is an incremental, relatively simple modification of the existing Density/Coverage (PRDC) framework rather than a fundamentally new evaluation paradigm.

The central interpretability claim (linear score degradation with proportion of "bad" samples) is one particular, somewhat idiosyncratic notion of interpretability; the paper does not deeply justify why this specific desideratum should be the gold standard versus alternative interpretable calibrations.

The human-correlation validation, a key piece of evidence for real-world validity, fails to show significance on FFHQ for both metrics, weakening the empirical case for correlation with human perceptual judgment on one of the four benchmark datasets.

In the comparison to the Räisä et al. (2025) benchmark, several failures of Clipped Coverage are explained away by the authors' own reinterpretation of what should count as a "pass" (Sections H.1/H.2), which, while reasonably argued, is somewhat self-serving and could be viewed skeptically by readers who trust the original benchmark's criteria.

Calibration for Clipped Coverage assumes the i.i.d. real=synthetic setting to derive the reference curve; robustness of this calibration when N and M differ substantially, or under more complex non-outlier distributional mismatches, is not deeply analyzed theoretically (only empirically for a few settings).

The paper explicitly acknowledges the lack of an infinite-sample theoretical analysis and does not exhaustively characterize all failure cases, relying on an evolving/incomplete battery of sanity checks.

The manuscript is extremely long (57 pages) with the vast majority of substantive evidence relegated to appendices; the main body alone (10 pages) provides comparatively limited direct empirical evidence, which could hinder standalone readability, though the appendix content is strong when read in full.
